newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU and U.S. hold new talks on product recognition.
newsitem.headline: EU and U.S. hold new talks on product recognition.

text.p: The European Union made fresh proposals to the United States on Tuesday in a bid to complete recently stalled talks over simplifying trade in pharmaceutical and other products, EU officials said.
EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan submitted the proposals to U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky at private talks on the sidelines of an OECD meeting, they said.
There were no details of the proposals and a U.S. official said no agreement was expected to be reached the same day.

Despite a stalemate in Washington talks last week, Brittan hoped to clinch an agreement soon so that pharmaceutical, medical and other products certified in the European Union would not need double-checking in the United States and vice-versa, EU officials said.

They said they had reached agreement on this so-called mutual recognition mechanism as far as telecommunications products, such as telephones and computers, were concerned and also on small electrical equipment, such as kitchen appliances.
But the sticking points proved to be pharmaceutical products and medical devices.
EU officials said Barshefsky would discuss Brittan's new proposals with the U.S. Food and Drugs Administration (FDA) and a second meeting was possible at the OECD later in the day.
EU officials said the FDA was reluctant to give up its powers to approve -- or reject -- European products.

One U.S. official close to last week's talks said that from the U.S. point of view the main sticking points were the EU demands on testing and certification of pharmaceuticals products and medical equipment, which the United States believed would lower U.S. consumer standards.
The EU hopes for a deal before U.S. President Bill Clinton meets European Commission President Jacques Santer on Wednesday.
An agreement across all sectors would concern trade in products worth an estimated 40 billion dollars, according to U.S. estimates, one EU official said.
